title: Non-Relational Database – New Notes
subtitle: Document, key-value, column-family, graph, Cosmos DB and partitioning — the critical model-vs-data distinction.

what.body: Non-relational describes the database MODEL: document, key-value, column-family or graph instead of tables joined by keys. It does NOT mean unstructured. Structured, semi-structured and unstructured describe the DATA: JSON is semi-structured data that often lives in a non-relational document database, while an image is unstructured data usually kept in blob storage.
what.example: A customer with name, email, several addresses, preferences and order history fits naturally in one JSON-like document instead of being forced across five fixed tables — especially when different customers carry different fields.

concepts.body: Modern apps often have data that changes frequently, nests information, or must spread across many machines. Document stores handle this naturally. Neither model is automatically better — the choice depends on the workload and data model.
Follows a predefined organization, commonly rows and columns: CustomerID | Name | Age | City. Examples: customer records, bank transactions, inventory.

No rigid table structure, but organized via keys, values, tags or nested objects. Examples: JSON, XML, HTML, logs, many email formats. Example: { "name": "Rahul", "age": 28, "skills": ["Python", "SQL"] }.
No predefined tabular or key-value model: images, videos, audio files, PDFs and other free-form documents. Commonly stored in object/blob storage.

Non-relational database != unstructured data. The database model (relational vs non-relational) and the data organization (structured vs semi-structured vs unstructured) are two separate exam questions. Always ask both: what kind of data is it, and what database model is used?
Document databases let different documents carry different fields — Document 1 has name + email, Document 2 adds phone + city. Useful when attributes evolve or records naturally differ.
Distributing data and workload across multiple machines instead of one bigger server. Many non-relational technologies are designed around distributed, scale-out workloads.
Stores JSON-like documents with nested objects and arrays. Good for product catalogs, user profiles, content management, mobile and web apps. Memory: document = documents / JSON-like data.
Each unique key maps to a value (101 -> Rahul), where the value can be a complex object. Good for caching, sessions, shopping carts and simple lookups. Memory: key -> value.

Organizes data into groups of related columns; built for large-scale distributed workloads. Examples: Apache Cassandra, Apache HBase. For DP-900, remember the idea (large distributed datasets), not implementation details.
Entities are nodes, relationships are edges, with properties on either. Good for social networks, recommendations, network analysis and fraud detection. Memory: graph = nodes + relationships.

Globally distributed Azure database for scalable apps, with multiple APIs/models: NoSQL/document, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin (graph) and Table. For exam questions: identify it as the globally distributed, multi-model service.

Very large data is split into partitions so storage and workload distribute (1 billion documents -> partition 1 + 2 + 3). The partition key (e.g. customerId) decides how data spreads. A bad key concentrates traffic/data on one hot partition.

Data fits documents/key-value/graph/column-family; schema must flex; very large or distributed scale; high throughput or low latency; data won't fit normalized tables; the model changes often. Relational still wins for strong relationships, fixed schemas, SQL and transactional workloads.

examples.title: The two-question trick
examples.body: Question 1: what kind of data? Structured, semi-structured or unstructured. Question 2: what database model? Relational or non-relational. JSON in Cosmos DB = semi-structured data + non-relational model. A photo in Blob storage = unstructured data + object storage, not a database at all.

services.name: Azure Cosmos DB
services.what: Globally distributed database service for scalable applications, with NoSQL/document, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin (graph) and Table APIs.
services.data: Semi-structured and model-specific data (JSON documents, graphs, key-values).
services.when: You need global distribution, elastic scale, or a specific API/model such as MongoDB or Gremlin.
services.scenario: Question says 'globally distributed Azure database' or names MongoDB / Cassandra / Gremlin / Table API on Azure.

remember: Non-relational = database MODEL. Structured/semi-structured/unstructured = DATA organization.
JSON/XML = semi-structured. Images, video, audio, PDFs = unstructured (blob storage).
Document = JSON-like (catalogs, profiles). Key-value = key -> value (cache, sessions, carts).
Column-family = groups of columns, huge distributed datasets (Cassandra, HBase).
Cosmos DB = globally distributed, multi-model: NoSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table.
Partition = split of data across machines. Partition key decides placement; bad key = hot partition.
Flexible schema: different documents may carry different fields.
Neither model is automatically better — match the workload and data model.

quickCheck.q: Is a JSON customer profile structured, semi-structured or unstructured?
quickCheck.a: Semi-structured — organized via keys and nesting, no rigid table schema.

quickCheck.q: Sessions and shopping carts need fast key lookups. Which model?
quickCheck.a: Key-value: each unique key maps to its value.

quickCheck.q: Users connected by friendships, plus fraud rings to detect. Which model?
quickCheck.a: Graph — nodes for entities, edges for relationships.

quickCheck.q: Globally distributed app using the MongoDB API on Azure?
quickCheck.a: Azure Cosmos DB — globally distributed with MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table and NoSQL APIs.

quickCheck.q: What decides how data spreads across partitions?
quickCheck.a: The partition key (e.g. customerId). A poor choice creates a hot partition.

quickCheck.q: One document has email only, another adds phone and city. What allows this?
quickCheck.a: Flexible schema in a document database — documents need not share identical fields.
